quizzes.question: Which of these earns a detail?
quizzes.explain: A detail holds what the video cannot: the evidence behind a number, never the number restated (style guide §20)

quizzes.question: You typed a comment, then press Esc. The words…
quizzes.explain: A6: Enter or Esc keeps the words and saves them to the record; only the × throws them away

autonomy.chose: The Open chip's key is O; while a question sheet is up, O keeps meaning "answer in my own words", so the chip waits behind it
autonomy.insteadOf: O opening the chip even over a question (or E, the plan's key)
autonomy.why: O is the chip's own first letter and is free outside a question; a question on screen owns its letters

autonomy.chose: Deviation from step 1: the Open chip's key is O
autonomy.insteadOf: Step 1 as written: the key is E
autonomy.why: E is Export today; moving Export would break a key reviewers and review-keys.spec.mjs already rely on

autonomy.chose: The panel is fixed to the window's right edge, full height, min(560px, 44vw) wide, and the stage shrinks beside it; where that would leave the stage under 640 px (a window under about 1250 px) or on a phone, it covers the window
autonomy.insteadOf: A panel inside the stage's own height, or an overlay on the stage
autonomy.why: A detail is read or tried at length: the stage's 16:9 height is too short for a page, and covering the stage would lose the frame it belongs to

autonomy.chose: Close plays again only if the video was playing when the detail opened and the playhead is still where it was; no seek back
autonomy.insteadOf: Always play on close, or always seek back to the opening moment
autonomy.why: "Resumes where you were": a reviewer who opened it from a paused frame, or moved the video while reading, would be surprised by a video that starts or jumps on its own

autonomy.chose: While the panel is open the video's keys are off (no play, draw or answer); O and Esc close it
autonomy.insteadOf: Letting space, A–D or N act on the hidden video
autonomy.why: Keys meant for the page should not start or answer the video under it. Once focus is inside the sandboxed page its keys are the page's own: Esc then works after one click on the panel's header, and × always works

autonomy.chose: A seventh template, fresh.html: the base styles, theme and bridge with an empty body, for kind fresh
autonomy.insteadOf: Writing the bridge from scratch each time
autonomy.why: The contract says a fresh page still carries the bridge; copying it is the reliable way

autonomy.chose: Data pages are filled by one JSON block (rp-data); a prototype by two slots, markup and behaviour; explore by one optional script
autonomy.insteadOf: HTML slots everywhere, or JSON only
autonomy.why: Data pages (table, evidence, code, plan text) are data; a prototype is markup and behaviour, and 90 steps are a loop, not a list

autonomy.chose: Each template's sample is the uploads plan (risks, the 8/16/32 MB staging runs, parts.ts line 14, before/after drop, manifest explorer, a step's text), marked "Sample content"
autonomy.why: A copied template already shows what good looks like for its kind; the check passes the templates as they are

autonomy.chose: A detail comment is kind: "note" with detail: { name, anchor, text }; Enter or Esc keeps the words, the × discards them; a click on another anchor keeps what was typed on the first
autonomy.insteadOf: A new kind (detail-note), or Esc discarding
autonomy.why: An ordinary annotation per the contract, so resolve-plan and every existing view read it as a comment; words are only thrown away on purpose

autonomy.chose: A click on a control (button, a, input, select, textarea, label, summary, [data-no-anchor]) inside an anchored element does not post an anchor; the anchor element itself does
autonomy.insteadOf: Posting an anchor on every click inside an anchor
autonomy.why: Sorting a table, copying a cell or pressing a prototype's button should not open a comment box; commenting on the region still works by clicking or selecting text in it

autonomy.chose: plan-text renders a Markdown link as its text plus the address in grey, never an <a href>
autonomy.why: The contract counts an http(s) href as a network load, and a sandboxed panel cannot open it anyway

autonomy.chose: Accept / Flag in the panel are one-shot like the sheet's: once a verdict is on the record the buttons show it and are disabled; if that call's sheet is waiting, the panel's verdict answers it too
autonomy.insteadOf: Letting the panel change a verdict, or leaving the sheet waiting
autonomy.why: The sheet has no "change" for a call either; one verdict per call keeps the export and the Flag note consistent

autonomy.chose: The plan text goes beside the stage (a 340 px column) when the stage loses under 10 % of its width for it; otherwise it is a section in the record, under Steps
autonomy.insteadOf: Always below the player in the page flow (the plan's words)
autonomy.why: The record sheet is fixed and rests at a peek that fills the window under the controls, so anything in the page flow below the player sits behind it; beside, the reviewer reads the lit step while the video plays

autonomy.chose: Deviation from step 5: the plan text sits beside the stage when the window is wide, in the record otherwise (A3)
autonomy.insteadOf: Step 5 as written: below the player
autonomy.why: The record sheet covers whatever sits below the player

autonomy.chose: The plan beside the video reads plan.md, never plan.resolved.md
autonomy.insteadOf: The resolved file when it exists
autonomy.why: The contract says plan.md; the resolved file appends review sections the page beside the video should not carry

autonomy.chose: The check fails on eight more ways a page can break than the four named before the build (the detail lists every rule)
autonomy.insteadOf: Only a missing page, a network load, missing bridge text, or a page error
autonomy.why: Each is a way the Open chip leads to a broken page; the last two test the bridge by running it, not by reading it

autonomy.chose: Without playwright-core (or when Chromium will not start) the static checks still run and the result says the pages were not opened
autonomy.why: The contract says "when available"; under npx the dev dependency is not installed

plan.title: Deep dives: the video opens into HTML where a video falls short
plan.problem:
A plan video is good at the story: the problem, the parts, each step, each choice. It is bad at
things you read at your own pace or poke at:

- **Code.** A diff, an API contract, a schema. The walkthrough says "check `src/upload/parts.ts`
  line 14", and the reviewer has to leave the player to find it.
- **Exact values and long lists.** A risk table, twelve config keys, every file a step touches. On
  screen for four seconds, they are gone before anyone reads them.
- **Things you try.** A layout, an animation, a flow. The Bob Dylan video shows design prototypes
  as pictures; you cannot click them.
- **Skimming, searching, copying.** The text plan sits next to the video, but nothing links the two.

HTML is good at exactly these ([The Unreasonable Effectiveness of HTML](https://thariqs.github.io/html-effectiveness/):
annotated PRs, plans with data-flow diagrams and risk tables, clickable prototypes). HTML alone is
still a page to read and scroll, which is why reelplanning chose video. This plan gets the pros of both:
the video tells the story, and any moment that needs more opens into HTML without leaving the player.

steps.title: Deep-dive beats
steps.text:
A storyboard beat can carry `- detail: <name>`, which points at a page in the video project's
`details/` folder. The plan map lists each detail with its frame, plan step and title. When the video
reaches a beat that has a detail, the player shows an "Open" chip (key: E). Opening it pauses the video
and shows the page. Closing it resumes where you were. The story never depends on a detail: the video
must make sense to someone who opens none.

steps.title: Kinds of detail, most of them things to try
steps.text:
**A detail must hold what the video cannot** (the reviewer's rule, second review): more than a screen can show, something to try,
or the evidence behind a claim. If one narrated sentence could say it, it is not a detail; say it in
the video. So most details are things you do, not things you read. For the resumable-uploads plan
and the Bob Dylan site, they would look like this:

- **Explore**: the frame's diagram, but live. Click a part to see what goes in and out; step through
  an upload yourself and watch the manifest row fill in, part 1 to part 90.
- **Try it**: a working prototype. Click through the three Bob Dylan home pages, drag the timeline,
  open an album. The design choice becomes three things you have used, not three pictures.
- **Evidence**: the data behind a number or a claim. The video says "16 MB parts lose less on a bad
  network"; the detail holds the staging runs behind it (8, 16 and 32 MB parts, each through the same
  forty dropped connections: parts resent, time to finish, retries), so the reviewer judges the number
  from the runs, not from the sentence.
- **Table**: anything with more than four rows. The risks, every config value, the options side by
  side. Sortable, and each cell copies.
- **Code**: only when the code itself is what you are judging: an API contract, a tricky function,
  a migration. Never by default (D-023).
- **Plan text**: the step as written in `plan.md`, so search and copy work.

The style guide carries the rule and its test: before adding a detail, write the one sentence the
video would say instead. If that sentence is enough, there is no detail. The narration says in one
sentence what opening it gives you that the video does not.

steps.title: Comments inside a detail
steps.text:
The review player's comment tools work in a detail. Select a line of code, a table row or an element
of a prototype and comment on it. The comment is tied to the plan step, the detail and the line or
row, and it reaches the agent like any other comment. resolve-plan lists it under its step with where
it points ("`parts.ts` line 14: …").

steps.title: Walkthroughs open onto what changed, not always the code
steps.text:
In a walkthrough, each call the agent made on its own can open a detail, and the detail shows whatever
lets you judge that call fastest (D-023):

- a behaviour change: a before-and-after you can try (the old upload failing at 90 %, the new one
  resuming);
- a value the agent picked: the evidence behind it, never just the value restated (the 16 MB part
  size opens onto the staging runs that chose it, next to the 8 MB the plan said);
- a change to an interface or to data: the code, with the lines that carry the call marked.

Code is one kind among these, used when the call is about the code itself. Accept and Flag work from
inside a detail as well as from the video.

steps.title: The whole plan as a page beside the video
steps.text:
Below the player, the full text of the plan, one section per step. The step the video is on is
highlighted, so you always know where you are in the text. Click any step and the video jumps there.
It is the text plan you would otherwise read on its own, joined to the video: you can skim ahead,
search for a word or copy a sentence without losing your place.

steps.title: Every detail works before you see it
steps.text:
Before a video reaches you, a check opens every detail it links to. A detail that is missing, broken,
or needs the internet to load stops the build, just as a broken frame does today. The review page you
open (on your machine or as a Claude page) carries the details with it, so an "Open" never leads
nowhere. This plan's own video is the first test: it is rebuilt with one detail of each kind.
